name: West Java
summary:
The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women in Indonesia: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026. Attackers punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers, and stripped some victims naked. Groups of 10–20 men filmed the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ("Bogor clean of LGBT"). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested, or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist accompanying women who filed police reports said officers "accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly." Additionally, 75 people were detained at a Puncak-area villa raid (June 2025) violating no law. Activists attribute the violence to Perpres 111/2025 classifying "LGBT culture" as a non-military threat, stating "people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the state has legitimised that violence."

This is well below the national score. Unlike Jakarta (0.12), where a discriminatory 56-man raid prompted immediate Amnesty demands and the detainees lacked legal charges, the Bogor wave shows patterned vigilante violence with total state inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.

name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
summary:
The largest LGBTQ+ community in Indonesia coincides with the biggest discriminatory police raids. On 1 February 2025 police arrested 56 men at a Jakarta hotel for a gathering that "violated no law"; the spokesperson dismissed it as "merely based on pleasure that they wanted to seek," and organisers risked prosecution under the pornography law with penalties up to 15 years. Amnesty International Indonesia stated the harassment "has no basis in law" and demanded immediate release. Jakarta is one of eight provinces where OutRight International documented discriminatory regional regulations. However, the city also hosts the densest LGBTQ+ infrastructure, media presence, and monitoring organisations (Arus Pelangi, Sekang).

The deviation from the national score is modest and below it. Unlike West Java (0.06), where patterned mob violence produced 45 victims with zero arrests and no institutional response, Jakarta's raids drew immediate civil-society pushback and lacked legal basis, limiting actual punishment exposure for a visitor. The combination of high enforcement activity and high community resilience nets a small negative.

name: West Sumatra
summary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh: Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024, articles 43–44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft ranperda on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines and "rehabilitation" for people of same-sex attraction. Academic analysis notes implementation remains weak precisely because rehabilitation facilities do not exist. West Sumatra also appears in OutRight's eight-province discriminatory-regulation analysis.

This sits below the national score because an enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines) that does not exist in most provinces. However, the documented absence of enforcement infrastructure and no recorded arrest or caning keep it above West Java (0.06), where patterned mob violence with zero accountability is the primary threat, and above the national floor where no such bylaw exists at all.

name: Bali
summary:
Bali offers the closest approximation to pockets of refuge in Indonesia: LGBTIQ+ people migrate there to "remake the meaning of home" and find spaces where they feel "valued, accepted and able to be themselves, even if those spaces are hidden and limited." No local enforcement actions, discriminatory bylaws, mass raids, or violence waves have been documented against trans visitors. The island sits outside OutRight's eight-province discriminatory-regulation set. However, the 2026 KUHP applies equally: Art. 412 criminalises sex outside marriage and cohabitation (up to one year, complaint-based by spouse/parent/child), and broad "indecency" provisions remain; travel guides discourage public displays of affection. A 2025 ethnographic study of transpuan communities in Bali explicitly challenges the "romanticised refuge" framing, documenting "resistance and misrecognition" and systemic discrimination even there.

The deviation above the national score reflects absent local enforcement rather than a legal exemption. Materially safer than Jakarta (0.12) with its hotel raids and discriminatory regs, but not a protected space; the new KUHP and Perpres 111/2025 create fresh exposure that could be activated in any police contact.

name: Papua
summary:
No trans-specific incident series was found for Papua, but the dossier documents 138 recorded acts of torture or other ill-treatment in detention committed by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and Q1 2025, "with almost no consequences." Named arbitrary-detention cases include three Papuans detained by officers at Nop Goliat Airport, Dekai (Yahukimo) on 26 July 2025 while one was boarding to study in Jayapura. Q3 2025 saw expanded military deployments and forced displacement. For any visitor, including a transgender one, the probability that police contact escalates into unlawful detention and ill-treatment is documented and far above the national average. This is an amplifier finding on non-trans-specific evidence, not an independent conclusion about trans people.

It sits at the same level as West Sumatra (0.11) in deviation from the national score, though the mechanism differs: West Sumatra has an enacted bylaw with specified administrative penalties; Papua has a documented torture-and-arrest pattern that raises the severity of any encounter with security forces, without a trans-specific legal basis being needed.

name: South Sulawesi
summary:
Makassar's mayor Munafri 'Appi' Arifuddin reaffirmed his commitment to pushing through an anti-LGBT Perda after a same-sex act at a night entertainment venue went viral; the deputy chair of the DPRD's legislation body backed it as "urgently needed to preserve moral order and religious norms." South Sulawesi is one of eight provinces in OutRight International's discriminatory-regulation analysis. No enacted bylaw with specified penalties yet exists, and no violence wave or mass police raid is documented in this province.

The small negative deviation from the national score reflects an active legislative push in a major domestic-tourism gateway to eastern Indonesia, raising the probability of future discriminatory enforcement. It remains above West Sumatra (0.11), where a Perda with articles 43–44 specifying fines and rehabilitation is already on the books, and above Jakarta (0.12), where a 56-person raid without legal basis has already occurred. The deviation is at the threshold because the law is proposed, not enacted, and per the enforcement-over-statute rule the traveler-facing impact is prospective.

name: South Sumatra
summary:
On 19 July 2026 the Palembang city government announced it was preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as follow-through on Presidential Regulation No. 111 of 2025, which lists the "spread of LGBTQ culture" among non-military threats to national defence alongside terrorism and trafficking. Mayor Ratu Dewa made the announcement in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque. South Sumatra also appears in OutRight's eight-province discriminatory-regulation set. The regulation remains in preparation, not yet enacted, with no specified penalty or enforcement event documented.

The deviation from the national score is small and below it, similar to South Sulawesi (0.13). The Perpres 111/2025 framing elevates local anti-LGBT rules from moral panic to national-defence doctrine—activists say this legitimised the Bogor mob violence—but without a specific enacted penalty the traveler-facing risk remains prospective. It sits above West Sumatra (0.11), which has a live bylaw with specified sanctions in articles 43–44, and above the national floor where no equivalent regulation has been announced.
